paper_metadata.title: Effects of Ta and Ti content on microstructure and properties of multicomponent Co-Ni-based superalloys

evidence.quote: Effects of Ta and Ti content on microstructure and properties of multicomponent Co – Ni-based superalloys
this paper studied the effects of Ta and Ti content on the microstructure and properties of γ′ phase strengthened nine-element Co–Ni-based casting superalloys.

As raw materials, the metals with high purity of 99.99% and above were used to prepare the experimental alloys by arc melting in argon atmosphere. To obtain uniform chemical composition, the alloys were repeatedly melted for 8 times. Finally, the button ingot was prepared with weight of about 20 g.

attributes.morphology: bright white contrast in BSE mode, interdendritic

evidence.quote: three kinds of interdendritic phases were preliminarily determined: Laves phase with bright white contrast in BSE mode, β phase with black contrast and (γ + γ′)e eutectic phase with grey contrast in BSE mode.

the large white-contrast interdendritic phase has a hexagonal structure (a ≈ 0.50 nm, c ≈ 0.75 nm, c/a ≈ 1.50). Combined with the composition analysis of EDS, it is Laves, possessing stoichiometric ratio conforms to (Co,Ni,Cr)2(Ta,Ti,Mo,Nb,W,Al).

evidence.section: 3.3. Solid solution and aging microstructure of alloys
evidence.quote: After solution treatment and recrystallization, the composition inside the grain of the experimental alloys is uniform. There is no secondary phase precipitation inside the grain or at the grain boundaries, and the interdendritic phase and dendrite structure in the as-cast microstructure have been completely eliminated

evidence.section: 3.5. Cost, density, mechanics and oxidation performance
evidence.quote: 4Ta1Ti alloys with the highest Ta content exactly has the highest room temperature Vickers hardness, while the highest Ti content alloys has the lowest room temperature Vickers hardness. When the Ta content decreases by 1 at% and the Ti content increases by 1 at%, the room temperature Vickers hardness of the aged experimental alloys decreases by 0.15 – 0.20 GPa.

evidence.section: 3.5. Cost, density, mechanics and oxidation performance
evidence.quote: The oxidation weight gain curve of the alloys after oxidation at 1050 ◦C for 10h and the surface morphology of the oxide layer under SEM backscatter mode are shown in Fig. 11. Alloys with the best oxidation resistance at 1050 ◦C are 2Ta3Ti alloys, and the oxidation resistance of the four alloys from high to low is 2Ta3Ti > 3Ta2Ti > 4Ta1Ti > 1Ta4Ti.

evidence.section: 3.5. Cost, density, mechanics and oxidation performance
evidence.quote: Besides, Ta element has a significant impact on the high-temperature mechanical properties of the alloys. With the content of 5 at% Ta and Ti, the compressive yield strength of the alloys decreases by an average of ~25 MPa at 1050 ◦C when Ta decreases by 1 at% and Ti increases by 1 at%.

The element Ti can increase the yield strength of the alloy by increasing the volume fraction of the γ′ phase [24], while when the Ti element content increases it causes the precipitation of the ŋ phase, which is detrimental to the microstructural stability of the alloy [25].
The enrichment Mo elements in the matrix plays a splendid solid solution strengthening effect, thus improving the mechanical properties of the alloys
